back: An earthquake releases stored **elastic energy** as **seismic waves**, which cause the shaking.

front: What does the **Moment Magnitude Scale** measure?
back: The Moment Magnitude Scale measures the **energy released** by an earthquake.

front: The Moment Magnitude Scale is <u>               </u>, so each whole-number increase means about 32 times more energy.
back: The Moment Magnitude Scale is **logarithmic**, so each whole-number increase means about 32 times more energy.

front: What does the **Mercalli Scale** measure?
back: The Mercalli Scale measures the **damage** that an earthquake causes.

front: Why does **magma** rise towards the surface?
back: Magma rises through cracks because of **buoyancy** and **gas pressure**.

front: Define **pyroclastic flow**.
back: A **pyroclastic flow** is a **fast-moving cloud** of hot gas, ash and rock fragments that can exceed **400°C**.

front:
**True or False?**

Carbon dioxide is the most common volcanic gas.
back:
**False.**

**Water vapour** is the most common volcanic gas.

front: How does volcanic **acid rain** form?
back: Volcanic acid rain forms when **sulfur dioxide (SO₂)** reacts with **water** in the atmosphere.

front: Define **volcanic bomb**.
back: A **volcanic bomb** is a large, **molten or semi-molten rock** ejected during an explosive eruption.

front:
**True or False?**

Volcanic ash only affects the area close to the volcano.
back:
**False.**

Ash can travel **globally** in the **upper atmosphere**.

front: Which scale measures the magnitude of a **volcanic eruption**?
back: The **Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI)** measures the magnitude of a volcanic eruption.

front: Why can volcanic **carbon dioxide** kill people?
back: Carbon dioxide can **collect in low-lying areas** and cause **suffocation**.

front: Why are **volcanic soils** fertile?
back: Volcanic materials weather into soils **rich in minerals**, such as **potassium, phosphorus, magnesium and iron**.

front: In geothermal power, steam extracted through wells drives <u>          </u> that generate electricity.
back: In geothermal power, steam extracted through wells drives **turbines** that generate electricity.

front:
**True or False?**

Geothermal energy from volcanic regions is a non-renewable energy source.
back:
**False.**

Geothermal energy is a **renewable** energy source that reduces reliance on **fossil fuels**.

front: Which **building materials** do volcanoes provide?
back: Volcanoes provide **basalt**, **pumice** and **scoria** for building and construction.

front: How do volcanoes make **minerals** easier to mine?
back: Hot volcanic fluids **deposit minerals in cracks and fissures**, bringing them **close to the surface**.

front: How does **volcanic tourism** benefit an area?
back: Volcanic tourism **creates jobs** for guides, hotels and restaurants and **boosts local and national economies**.

front: Define **primary hazard**.
back: A **primary hazard** is a **direct result** of an earthquake or volcanic eruption.

front: Define **secondary hazard**.
back: A **secondary hazard** occurs **as a result of the primary effects** of an earthquake or eruption.

front: Which **factors** affect the impacts of a tectonic event?
back: Impacts depend on **magnitude**, **distance** from the epicentre or volcano, **population density**, **building quality** and **preparedness**.

front: Define **lahar**.
back: A **lahar** is a **mudflow** that forms when volcanic ash mixes with water.

front: Why do airlines cancel flights near a **volcanic ash cloud**?
back: Flying through ash clouds can cause **jet engine failure**.

front: Poor <u>             </u> in evacuation shelters increases the risk of water-related disease after a tectonic event.
back: Poor **sanitation** in evacuation shelters increases the risk of water-related disease after a tectonic event.

front: How do **earthquakes** cause fires?
back: Earthquakes cause fires when **ruptured gas lines** ignite.

front: What are the three **phases** of managing a tectonic hazard?
back: The three phases are **before** the event (preparation), **during** the event (survival and protection) and **after** the event (recovery and rebuilding).

front: Which instrument records **ground movement** during an earthquake?
back: A **seismometer** records ground movement during an earthquake.

front: Earthquake warning systems detect the initial <u>         </u> and send alerts seconds before the shaking arrives.
back: Earthquake warning systems detect the initial **P-waves** and send alerts seconds before the shaking arrives.

front:
**True or False?**

Scientists can predict the exact time of an earthquake.
back:
**False.**

Scientists **cannot predict earthquakes accurately**; warning systems give only **seconds** of warning.

front: How do scientists measure **ground deformation** at a volcano?
back: Scientists measure ground deformation with **GPS** and **tiltmeters**.

front: Define **land use zoning**.
back: **Land use zoning** is when planning authorities **restrict development** in high-risk zones.

front: Why is **land use zoning** difficult to enforce?
back: Zoning is difficult to enforce where **land is scarce**, people **build illegally** and **existing settlements** cannot easily move.

front: How does **base isolation** protect a building in an earthquake?
back: Base isolation uses **rubber bearings** to reduce the transfer of **ground movement** into the building.

front: Cross-bracing prevents earthquake-resistant buildings from <u>          </u> or buckling.
back: Cross-bracing prevents earthquake-resistant buildings from **twisting** or buckling.

front: Why do buildings in volcanic areas have **steep roofs**?
back: Steep roofs **prevent ash from accumulating**, so the roof does not collapse.

front:
**True or False?**

All countries can adopt earthquake-resistant building designs equally easily.
back:
**False.**

These designs **cost a lot to build**, so **high-income countries (HICs)** adopt them far more easily.

front: Which volcanic hazard overwhelms **all building designs**?
back: **Pyroclastic flows** overwhelm all building structures.

front: What does **disaster preparation** aim to do?
back: Disaster preparation aims to **reduce panic** and **improve survival**.

front:
**True or False?**

Evacuation drills stay effective however rarely people practise them.
back:
**False.**

Drills may be **ineffective** if they happen **too infrequently**.

front: Why might people **refuse to evacuate** before a tectonic event?
back: People may refuse to evacuate because they do not want to **leave their livelihoods behind**.

front: How do **emergency shelters** reduce disease outbreaks?
back: Shelters provide **food, water, sanitation and medical care** for displaced people.

front: What is a limitation of **emergency shelters**?
back: Shelters can become **overcrowded** or **under-supplied**, and long-term sheltering harms **mental and physical health**.

front:
**True or False?**

Relying on international aid always speeds up local recovery.
back:
**False.**

**Reliance on aid** can **slow local recovery**, and aid may also arrive too late.

front: Which stage of tectonic hazard management usually **costs the most**?
back: **Rebuilding** is usually the stage that costs the most, and it can take years.

front: Rebuilding after a tectonic event offers a chance to improve <u>                         </u>.
back: Rebuilding after a tectonic event offers a chance to improve **building standards**.

front: Which forms of **international aid** help after a tectonic disaster?
back: International aid includes **emergency supplies**, **rescue and medical teams**, **long-term financial support** for rebuilding and **technical expertise** for monitoring.

front: What can stop **international aid** from reaching people?
back: **Political tensions** or **corruption** can hinder the distribution of aid.

front: Define **tropical cyclone**.
back: A **tropical cyclone** is a **rotating, intense low-pressure system**.

front:
**True or False?**

Each regional name for a tropical cyclone describes a different type of storm.
back:
**False.**

All the regional names describe the **same type of storm**; only the **name varies by region**.

front: What are tropical cyclones called in the **Caribbean Sea**?
back: Tropical cyclones in the Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico are called **hurricanes**.

front: Tropical cyclones in the South China Sea and the western Pacific Ocean are called <u>          </u>.
back: Tropical cyclones in the South China Sea and the western Pacific Ocean are called **typhoons**.

front: Between which **latitudes** do tropical cyclones form?
back: Tropical cyclones form between **5° and 30°** north or south of the Equator.

front: Why do tropical cyclones not form **at the Equator**?
back: The **Coriolis effect** is too weak at the Equator to make the storm spin.

front: Tropical cyclones need an ocean temperature of at least <u>    </u>.
back: Tropical cyclones need an ocean temperature of at least **27°C**.

front: Why do tropical cyclones not form at **higher latitudes**?
back: Tropical cyclones do not form at higher latitudes because the **water is too cold**.

front:
**True or False?**

Tropical cyclones form when an undersea earthquake disturbs the ocean.
back:
**False.**

Tropical cyclones form over **warm tropical oceans**, which supply the **heat energy** that drives the storm.

front: Why must warm water extend to a **depth of 60 m**?
back: Deep warm water lets the storm **keep gaining energy** without **mixing with cooler water** from below.

front: How does **warm ocean water** strengthen a tropical cyclone?
back: Warm water **evaporates rapidly**, adding **heat and moisture** to the rising air; more evaporation releases more **latent heat**, which makes the cyclone stronger.

front: When in the year do **tropical cyclones** form?
back: Tropical cyclones form when tropical oceans are **warmest**: **June-November** in the northern hemisphere and **November-April** in the southern hemisphere.

front: Which **ocean** has the most tropical storms?
back: The **Pacific Ocean** has the most tropical storms, followed by the Indian Ocean and then the Atlantic.

front:
**True or False?**

Storm surges are the only cause of flooding during a tropical cyclone.
back:
**False.**

**Torrential rain** and **overflowing rivers** also cause flooding, alongside storm surges.

front: Which hazards combine to make **tropical cyclones** so damaging?
back: Tropical cyclones combine **high winds**, **intense rainfall**, **storm surges** and **flooding**.

front: How do **storm surges** damage farmland?
back: Storm surges bring **saltwater** onto farmland, which **ruins the soil** for crops.

front: How do tropical cyclones trigger **landslides**?
back: **Heavy rainfall saturates slopes**, which triggers landslides.

front: Standing water after a tropical cyclone encourages <u>          </u> breeding.
back: Standing water after a tropical cyclone encourages **mosquito** breeding.

front: How do tropical cyclones contaminate **drinking water**?
back: **Floodwater mixes sewage** with clean water, and **saline intrusion** from storm surges pollutes wells and aquifers.

front: Which **financial losses** do tropical cyclones cause?
back: Tropical cyclones cause **repair costs** for transport, homes, utilities and businesses, plus **lost farm production** and **lost tourism** income.

front: Which methods do agencies use to **monitor** tropical cyclones?
back: Agencies use **satellite images**, **radar and wind measurements**, **aircraft reconnaissance** and **computer modelling**.

front: Computer modelling helps forecasters predict a tropical cyclone's <u>    </u>.
back: Computer modelling helps forecasters predict a tropical cyclone's **path**.

front: Which **storm surge** measurement can forecasts predict?
back: Forecasts can predict storm surge **height**, which helps coastal areas prepare for flooding.

front:
**True or False?**

Tropical cyclone warnings always reach every community.
back:
**False.**

Some **remote communities** may **not receive warnings**.

front: How can changing **forecasts** weaken a warning system?
back: Predictions may change, which **reduces public trust** in later warnings.

front: How do **hurricane straps** protect a building?
back: Hurricane straps **secure the roof** so high winds cannot rip it off.

front: Define **cyclone shelter**.
back: A **cyclone shelter** is a **strong, elevated structure** of reinforced concrete that protects large groups of people and stores food, water and medicine.

front:
**True or False?**

Extreme cyclone winds cannot destroy reinforced buildings.
back:
**False.**

**Extreme winds** can **still destroy** reinforced structures.

front: Why do **low-income communities** often lack wind-resistant buildings?
back: Low-income communities often **cannot afford** the improvements, and **upgrading old buildings** costs a lot of money.

front: Which areas do people **evacuate** from before a tropical cyclone?
back: People evacuate from **low-lying coasts** and **landslide-prone hills**.

front: What can delay a cyclone **evacuation**?
back: **Traffic congestion** delays movement, and some people **refuse to leave**.

front:
**True or False?**

Cyclone shelters protect everyone in a cyclone-prone area.
back:
**False.**

Shelters can become **overcrowded**, have **poor conditions** and are **not accessible to everyone**.

front: What does **disaster preparation** for tropical cyclones include?
back: Preparation includes **emergency plans and evacuation routes**, **community drills**, **stockpiled supplies**, **trained rescue teams** and **public education campaigns**.

front: Why can **disaster preparation** fail to protect a community?
back: Preparation needs **regular training and funding**, not all communities take part, and supplies may **not be maintained** properly.

front: Rebuilding after a tropical cyclone offers an opportunity to upgrade <u>                         </u>.
back: Rebuilding after a tropical cyclone offers an opportunity to upgrade **building standards**.

front: Why is **rebuilding** after a tropical cyclone difficult?
back: Rebuilding is **slow** and costs a great deal of money, **insurance** may not cover all the costs, and it can **disrupt communities**.

front: Which forms of **international aid** help after a tropical cyclone?
back: Aid includes **emergency supplies**, **medical teams and rescue workers**, **financial assistance** for rebuilding and **planning expertise**.

front: Damaged <u>                      </u> can delay international aid.
back: Damaged **transport routes** can delay international aid.

front:
**True or False?**

International aid has no long-term drawbacks.
back:
**False.**

Aid can **create dependency** in the long term, and some aid may be **poorly managed or misused**.

front: Why was large-scale evacuation limited during **Cyclone Idai** (2019)?
back: **Poverty** and **damaged infrastructure** limited evacuation, and **poor communication** weakened the early warning.

front: When does a **river** flood?
back: A river floods when the **volume of water** is greater than the river's **capacity**.

front: Define **saturated soil**.
back: **Saturated soil** is soil that already holds as much water as it can, so it **cannot absorb any more**.

front: Why do **steep slopes** increase flood risk?
back: On steep slopes, rainwater flows quickly downhill and has **no time to infiltrate**, so river levels rise sharply.

front: Urbanisation covers land with <u>               </u> surfaces, such as roads and rooftops, that stop water soaking into the ground.
back: Urbanisation covers land with **impermeable** surfaces, such as roads and rooftops, that stop water soaking into the ground.

front: Why does **compacted soil** increase surface run-off?
back: Compacted soil has fewer **air spaces** to store water, so even light rain becomes surface run-off.

front:
**True or False?**

Storm surges and tsunamis are mainly causes of river flooding.
back:
**False.**

Storm surges and tsunamis are **coastal** flooding causes, so they affect **coastlines** rather than river systems.

front: How does **deforestation** increase flood risk?
back: Deforestation removes trees that **intercept rainfall**, so more water runs quickly into rivers.

front: Define **storm surge**.
back: A **storm surge** is a temporary **rise in sea level** that forms when powerful winds push seawater towards the coast.

front: Why does **climate change** bring heavier rainfall?
back: Climate change brings heavier rainfall because **warmer air holds more moisture**, so storms carry extra water.

front: Higher sea levels mean storm surges start from a higher point, so they travel further <u>       </u>.
back: Higher sea levels mean storm surges start from a higher point, so they travel further **inland**.

front: Define **tsunami**.
back: A **tsunami** is a giant wave that forms when an **underwater earthquake, volcanic eruption or landslide** displaces a huge volume of water.

front:
**True or False?**

All the impacts of a flood are short-term.
back:
**False.**

Some flood impacts are **long-term** and last months or years, such as **soil too damaged to grow food**.

front: How does floodwater kill **crops**?
back: Floodwater kills crops by covering them for too long, which stops them getting the **oxygen** they need.

front: How do floods contaminate **drinking water**?
back: Floods contaminate drinking water when **sewage systems overflow** and when **chemicals leak** from factories, petrol stations and farms into the floodwater.

front: Stagnant water after a flood creates breeding sites for <u>             </u>, which spread malaria and dengue fever.
back: Stagnant water after a flood creates breeding sites for **mosquitoes**, which spread malaria and dengue fever.

front: How can heavy rain trigger a **landslide**?
back: Heavy rain soaks into hillside soil, making it **heavier** and more likely to **slip downhill**.

front: Why can flooded homes cause **respiratory problems**?
back: Damp, flooded homes grow **mould**, which makes the air unhealthy to breathe.

front:
**True or False?**

Landslides caused by flooding lower the risk of future floods.
back:
**False.**

Landslides **destroy vegetation**, so the soil loses **root support** and future flood risk increases.

front: Why do floods strain **government budgets**?
back: Floods strain government budgets because governments must pay for **rebuilding roads, bridges and public services**.

front: Which **nutrients** does flood silt add to farmland?
back: Flood silt adds nutrients such as **nitrogen** and **phosphorus** to farmland.

front: How does flood silt reduce farmers' spending on **fertiliser**?
back: Flood silt makes the soil more **fertile**, so farmers need to **buy less fertiliser**.

front: Some floodwater soaks through the soil into <u>          </u>, which are natural underground water stores.
back: Some floodwater soaks through the soil into **aquifers**, which are natural underground water stores.

front: How do scientists **monitor** flood risk?
back: Scientists monitor rainfall, river levels and weather patterns using **satellites, sensors and computers**.

front: Define **land use zoning**.
back: **Land use zoning** is the use of maps to identify **high-risk flood zones** and decide which activities are allowed there.

front: Land use zoning places hospitals and emergency centres on <u>       </u> ground, where they are less likely to flood.
back: Land use zoning places hospitals and emergency centres on **higher** ground, where they are less likely to flood.

front: How can **building design** keep living areas above floodwater?
back: Builders raise homes on **stilts** or **raised foundations** to keep living areas above floodwater.

front: Why do builders place **electrical sockets** high on walls in flood-prone areas?
back: Builders place electrical sockets high on walls so they **stay dry and safe** during floods.

front: Define **disaster preparation**.
back: **Disaster preparation** is getting communities ready for a flood through **plans, drills, emergency supplies and rescue teams**.

front: Why do planners set **evacuation routes** in advance?
back: Planners set evacuation routes in advance to **avoid roads that may flood first**.

front: Flood shelters reduce the risk of illness because <u>         </u> is easier to control there than in flooded homes.
back: Flood shelters reduce the risk of illness because **hygiene** is easier to control there than in flooded homes.

front: How can **rebuilding** reduce future flood damage?
back: Rebuilding can make structures **stronger and more flood-resistant**, for example by **raising roads** and **widening drains**.

front: What does **international aid** provide after severe flooding?
back: International aid provides **emergency food, medicine, clean water, tents and rescue teams**, plus money to rebuild homes, infrastructure and schools.

front:
**True or False?**

Flood monitoring and warning technology always works, even during storms.
back:
**False.**

Monitoring technology can **fail in storms** or in **remote areas**.

front: What must people do for **flood warnings** to be useful?
back: Flood warnings are only useful when people **understand and trust** them.

front:
**True or False?**

Land use zoning is easy to introduce in older settlements.
back:
**False.**

Zoning is **hard to introduce** where older settlements are **already built on floodplains**.

front: How does **land use zoning** let floodplains reduce flood damage?
back: Zoning keeps floodplains free of buildings, so they can **absorb water naturally**.

front: Why is flood-resistant **building design** hard for poorer communities to adopt?
back: Raising or adapting buildings has **high building costs** that poorer communities often **cannot afford**.

front:
**True or False?**

Everyone can leave quickly once a flood evacuation begins.
back:
**False.**

**Elderly or disabled people** may struggle to leave quickly.

front: What does **disaster preparation** need in order to keep working?
back: Disaster preparation needs **regular funding, training and community participation**.

front: Why can **flood shelters** struggle during large floods?
back: Flood shelters have **limited space and resources** during large floods.

front: Why can **rebuilding** fail to reduce future flood risk?
back: Rebuilding in the same **high-risk areas** may simply **repeat the problem**.

front: Long-term dependence on international aid can weaken local <u>             </u>.
back: Long-term dependence on international aid can weaken local **resilience**.

front: Why can **international aid** slow flood recovery?
back: International aid can slow recovery because it **may take time to arrive**.

front: Define **drought**.
back: A **drought** is a period of dry weather that is **longer or more severe than normal** for a particular region.

front:
**True or False?**

A drought means a period with no rain at all.
back:
**False.**

A drought means water levels have fallen **below what people, crops and ecosystems need**, not simply that no rain falls.

front: Which two **water stores** does drought affect?
back: Drought affects **surface water**, such as rivers and lakes, and **groundwater** in aquifers.

front: Compared with cyclones or floods, a drought develops <u>       </u>.
back: Compared with cyclones or floods, a drought develops **slowly**.

front: How do **high-pressure systems** cause drought?
back: High-pressure systems **block clouds** and prevent rainfall.

front: How do **higher global temperatures** make droughts worse?
back: Higher temperatures increase **evaporation** from soil, plants and water bodies, so moisture is lost faster than rain can replace it.

front:
**True or False?**

Climate change makes rainfall more reliable.
back:
**False.**

Climate change brings **more extreme weather**, so rainfall becomes **unreliable**, with floods one year and long dry spells the next.

front: How do **warmer oceans** contribute to drought?
back: Warmer oceans **disrupt wind patterns and monsoons**, which can move rain-bearing winds away and reduce rainfall.

front: During a drought, groundwater levels fall because aquifers are not being <u>            </u>.
back: During a drought, groundwater levels fall because aquifers are not being **recharged**.

front: Which type of **power station** may stop working during a drought?
back: **Hydroelectric** power stations may stop working during a drought.

front: Why does drought lead to **soil erosion**?
back: Without vegetation, dry soil is **not anchored**, so wind blows it away and sudden rainstorms wash away topsoil.

front: Define **desertification**.
back: **Desertification** is the process by which long-term drought turns fertile land into **desert-like conditions**.

front: Which **human activities** speed up desertification?
back: **Overgrazing** and **deforestation** speed up desertification.

front:
**True or False?**

Wildfire risk falls during a drought.
back:
**False.**

Wildfire risk rises because dry vegetation becomes **highly flammable**.

front: Why can drought cause **famine**?
back: **Crop failure** and **livestock losses** reduce the food supply, and food prices rise so vulnerable communities **cannot afford food**.

front: In a drought, grass and fodder run short, so livestock weaken and die from heat stress or <u>               </u>.
back: In a drought, grass and fodder run short, so livestock weaken and die from heat stress or **dehydration**.

front: Why does drought reduce **air quality**?
back: Drought makes **dust storms** more frequent and fills the air with **smoke from wildfires**.

front: Why does drought increase **government spending**?
back: Governments must spend money on **food aid** and **water supplies** during a drought.

front:
**True or False?**

The health impacts of a drought end as soon as rain returns.
back:
**False.**

Drought can leave **long-term health challenges**, such as malnutrition and mental health impacts, even after rainfall returns.

front: How can a long drought affect **food chains**?
back: A long drought kills plants, fish and wildlife, so **whole food chains can collapse** and biodiversity falls.

front: Define **igneous rock**.
back: **Igneous rock** is rock that forms when **molten rock** (magma or lava) cools and solidifies.

front: How does **magma** differ from **lava**?
back: Magma is molten rock **beneath the Earth's surface**, while lava is molten rock that **reaches the surface**.

front: Define **intrusive igneous rock**.
back: **Intrusive igneous rock** forms **below the surface** when magma cools **slowly**, so it has **large crystals**, for example granite.

front:
**True or False?**

Igneous rocks are soft and erode easily.
back:
**False.**

Igneous rocks are **hard** and **more resistant to erosion**.

front: Define **extrusive igneous rock**.
back: **Extrusive igneous rock** forms **on the surface** when lava cools **quickly**, so it has **small crystals**, for example basalt.

front: Basalt is a dark, fine-grained rock found mainly in <u>         </u> crust.
back: Basalt is a dark, fine-grained rock found mainly in **oceanic** crust.

front: Define **sedimentary rock**.
back: **Sedimentary rock** forms from **sediments** that are eroded, transported and deposited, then **compacted and cemented** over time.

front: What is **limestone** mainly made of?
back: Limestone is mainly made of **calcium carbonate** from the **shells and skeletons** of marine organisms.

front: Sandstone forms from sand-sized grains, mainly <u>       </u>, that are buried, compacted and cemented.
back: Sandstone forms from sand-sized grains, mainly **quartz**, that are buried, compacted and cemented.

front: Which particles form **shale**?
back: Shale forms from **clay and silt particles** that settle in **calm water**, such as lakes or deep seas.

front: Define **metamorphic rock**.
back: **Metamorphic rock** is **existing igneous or sedimentary rock** changed by **heat and/or pressure** inside the Earth.

front: Which metamorphic rock forms when **limestone** recrystallises under heat and pressure?
back: **Marble** forms when the calcium carbonate crystals in limestone recrystallise.

front:
**True or False?**

Metamorphic rocks form when existing rock melts and then cools.
back:
**False.**

Metamorphism changes rock through heat, pressure or chemical processes **without melting** it.

front: Which metamorphic rock forms when the minerals in **shale** align into thin layers?
back: **Slate** forms when moderate heat and pressure align the minerals in shale.

front: Define **rock cycle**.
back: The **rock cycle** is a **continuous process** that shows how rocks **change from one type to another** over time.

front: Define **weathering**.
back: **Weathering** is the **breakdown of rocks in situ**, at or near the Earth's surface, into smaller pieces.

front: How does **acid rain** cause chemical weathering?
back: Acid rain causes chemical weathering through **chemical reactions** that **dissolve minerals** in rocks.

front: Freeze-thaw action is a type of <u>          </u> weathering.
back: Freeze-thaw action is a type of **physical** weathering.

front: Define **erosion**.
back: **Erosion** is the **removal** of weathered rock particles from their **original location**.

front:
**True or False?**

Plant roots growing into cracks cause chemical weathering.
back:
**False.**

Plant roots and animals breaking down rock cause **biological weathering**.

front: Define **transportation**.
back: **Transportation** is the **movement of eroded material** (sediment) from one place to another by wind, rivers, glaciers or waves.

front: Which **sediment particles** travel furthest during transportation?
back: **Smaller, lighter particles** travel furthest, while larger, heavier particles move only short distances.

front: Define **deposition**.
back: **Deposition** is the **dropping of sediment** after transport, when the moving water, wind or ice **loses energy** and can no longer carry it.

front: Which **landforms** does deposition create?
back: Deposition creates landforms such as **river deltas**, **sand dunes** and **beaches**.

front: Define **sedimentation**.
back: **Sedimentation** is the process by which transported material **settles and builds up in layers** at the bottom of rivers, lakes and oceans.

front:
**True or False?**

Sedimentation happens before deposition.
back:
**False.**

Sedimentation starts **after deposition**, once dropped sediment begins to collect in layers.

front: Define **compaction**.
back: **Compaction** is when **pressure from the sediment layers above** squeezes the lower layers together.

front: During compaction, <u>                  </u> are pushed out from between the grains, so the sediment becomes denser.
back: During compaction, **water and air** are pushed out from between the grains, so the sediment becomes denser.

front: Define **cementation**.
back: **Cementation** is when minerals **crystallise and glue compacted particles together** to form sedimentary rock.

front: Which minerals bind sediment grains together during **cementation**?
back: Minerals such as **silica** or **calcium carbonate** fill the spaces between grains and bind them together.

front: Define **crystallisation**.
back: **Crystallisation** is the process by which **molten rock cools and forms crystals**, making igneous rock.

front:
**True or False?**

Rapid cooling of lava on the surface produces large crystals.
back:
**False.**

Rapid cooling produces **small crystals**, as in basalt; **slow cooling underground** produces large crystals, as in granite.

front: Define **permeability**.
back: **Permeability** is the ability of **water to pass through the pore spaces** of rock and soil.

front: Define **pore spaces**.
back: **Pore spaces** are the **tiny gaps** between rock or soil particles that let water and air move through.

front:
**True or False?**

A porous rock is always permeable.
back:
**False.**

Porous means the rock has spaces; if those **pores are not connected**, water cannot flow through, so the rock is **impermeable**.

front: Why are most **sedimentary rocks** permeable?
back: Most sedimentary rocks are permeable because they form from **layers of particles** that leave **spaces between the grains**.

front: Two examples of permeable rocks are limestone and <u>            </u>.
back: Two examples of permeable rocks are limestone and **sandstone**.

front: Why does **limestone** let water flow through it?
back: Limestone lets water flow through because it has **small cracks and spaces**.

front: Define **aquifer**.
back: An **aquifer** is an **underground layer of permeable rock** that stores groundwater.

front: Why are **igneous** and **metamorphic** rocks usually impermeable?
back: Igneous and metamorphic rocks are usually impermeable because they have a **dense, compact structure** with **few spaces** for water.

front:
**True or False?**

Shale is a permeable sedimentary rock.
back:
**False.**

Shale is **impermeable** because its **fine clay particles** pack tightly together.

front: What happens to water that reaches an **impermeable rock**?
back: The water cannot soak in, so it **flows over the surface** or **collects above the rock**, forming springs or surface water.

front: Define **ore**.
back: An **ore** is a rock that contains **minerals and metals** that people can **extract and use**.

front: Which **ore** provides aluminium?
back: **Bauxite** is the ore that provides aluminium.

front: Define **surface extraction**.
back: **Surface extraction** is the removal of rocks, ores and minerals from **close to the Earth's surface**, also called open mining.

front: Define **overburden**.
back: The **overburden** is the **worthless rock and soil** that opencast mining removes to reach the valuable material beneath.

front: What environmental damage can **surface extraction** cause?
back: Surface extraction can cause **large-scale damage to the landscape and habitats**.

front: Define **subsurface extraction**.
back: **Subsurface extraction** is the removal of rocks, ores and minerals from **deep below the Earth's surface**, where deposits are too deep for surface mining.

front:
**True or False?**

Subsurface extraction costs less to run than surface extraction.
back:
**False.**

Subsurface extraction costs more because mines need **ventilation**, **drainage systems** and **strong supports**; surface extraction is often cheaper.

front: How does **deep mining** reach a mineral deposit?
back: In deep mining, workers dig **tunnels** to reach the deposit and remove the rock **from below**.

front: In shaft mining, vertical shafts give access to the mineral layers, and <u>                     </u> bring materials to the surface.
back: In shaft mining, vertical shafts give access to the mineral layers, and **lifts or hoists** bring materials to the surface.

front: Which safety risks do workers face in **subsurface extraction**?
back: Workers in subsurface extraction face **cave-ins**, **gas leaks** and **poor air quality**.

front: Define **biological extraction**.
back: **Biological extraction** is the use of **living organisms** to extract metals from ores.

front: Define **phytomining**.
back: **Phytomining** is a method in which **plants absorb metal ions** from the soil, then people harvest and burn the plants to get metal compounds from the **ash**.

front:
**True or False?**

Biological extraction is a fast way to obtain metals.
back:
**False.**

Biological extraction is a **slow process**, although it uses **less energy** than traditional mining.

front: Define **bioleaching**.
back: **Bioleaching** is a method in which **bacteria** feed on the minerals in an ore and produce a **solution containing metal ions**.

front: Which type of **ore** can biological extraction use that would otherwise go to waste?
back: Biological extraction can use **low-grade ores** that miners would otherwise waste.

front: Define **exploration**.
back: **Exploration** is the **search for areas** where valuable minerals or rocks occur.

front: Which methods does modern **exploration** use?
back: Modern exploration uses **drilling**, **sampling** and **satellite surveys**.

front:
**True or False?**

Extraction is always worthwhile once exploration finds a deposit.
back:
**False.**

If the deposit is **too small** or **too deep**, extraction may not be worthwhile.

front: Why are minerals in **igneous** or **metamorphic** rocks harder to extract than those in sedimentary rocks?
back: Minerals in igneous or metamorphic rocks are harder to extract because **hard or folded rocks** cost more to mine than **softer, layered** sedimentary rocks.

front: Define **accessibility**.
back: **Accessibility** is **how easy it is to reach** a mining site.

front: Which type of **terrain** is easiest to mine?
back: **Flat or gently sloping land** is easier and cheaper to mine than steep or uneven terrain.

front: Define **ore grade**.
back: **Ore grade** is the **concentration** of the metal or mineral in the rock.

front:
**True or False?**

Low-grade ores cost less to process than high-grade ores.
back:
**False.**

Low-grade ores produce **less metal** and need **more processing**, which raises costs.

front: In a wet climate, heavy rainfall can cause <u>          </u> in open pits or underground tunnels.
back: In a wet climate, heavy rainfall can cause **flooding** in open pits or underground tunnels.

front: How can a **dry climate** affect mining?
back: A dry climate can create **dust pollution**, which harms **air quality and health**.

front: Define **Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)**.
back: An **Environmental Impact Assessment** is a **study that takes place before a project starts** to understand how it will affect land, water, air, plants and animals.

front: What can happen to a mining proposal if its **EIA** predicts severe environmental damage?
back: If the EIA predicts severe damage, the government may **limit** or **refuse** extraction.

front: Which **supply and demand** conditions make a mineral most profitable to extract?
back: **High demand** and **low supply** make a mineral most profitable to extract.

front:
**True or False?**

A mine always keeps operating once extraction has started.
back:
**False.**

If **demand falls** or **alternative materials** replace the mineral, mining may stop because it is no longer profitable.

front: When does **cost** stop a mining project from going ahead?
back: A mining project will not go ahead if its **costs are greater than its expected profits**.

front: Why does mining reduce **biodiversity**?
back: Mining removes large areas of **vegetation and topsoil**, which **destroys habitats** and so reduces biodiversity.

front:
**True or False?**

Habitats recover quickly after open-pit mining ends.
back:
**False.**

Recovery is **slow** because mining often removes or contaminates the **soil and nutrients**.

front: Which gases do mining **machinery and vehicles** release?
back: Mining machinery and vehicles release **carbon dioxide** and **sulfur dioxide**.

front: Dust from blasting, digging and transporting materials causes <u>                  </u> around mines.
back: Dust from blasting, digging and transporting materials causes **air pollution** around mines.

front: Define **land pollution** from mining.
back: **Land pollution** from mining happens when mines **dump waste rock and chemicals** on the ground, which can make soil infertile.

front:
**True or False?**

Noise from mining affects only the workers on site.
back:
**False.**

Noise from **blasting, drilling and heavy machinery** also affects **local wildlife** and **nearby communities**.

front: Define **acid mine drainage**.
back: **Acid mine drainage** happens when **rainwater reacts with exposed rock**, releasing acids and metals into water sources.

front: What causes **visual pollution** at mines?
back: Visual pollution comes from **large mines and waste heaps**, which change the landscape and spoil natural scenery.

front: Why can mining **water use** cause problems in dry areas?
back: Mining uses large amounts of water for **cooling, processing and dust control**, which leaves **less water for people, animals and farming**.

front: Define **tailings**.
back: **Tailings** are the **leftover materials** from ore once processing has removed the valuable minerals.

front: How can mines reduce the environmental risk from **tailings**?
back: Mines can reduce the risk by storing tailings in **properly lined and managed waste ponds**.

front: How does mining benefit a **national economy**?
back: Mining **increases exports** and generates **tax revenue** for the government.

front: Mining towns can suffer <u>                </u> once resources run out or demand for the mineral falls.
back: Mining towns can suffer **unemployment** once resources run out or demand for the mineral falls.

front:
**True or False?**

Mining profits always stay in the local community.
back:
**False.**

Profits may go to **foreign companies** rather than local communities.

front: Why might **local people** miss out on new mining jobs?
back: Mining jobs can need **skilled workers**, and local people may lack the **right skills or training**.

front: When can mining profits **increase inequality**?
back: Mining profits can increase inequality when **unfair sharing** of the money widens the gap between rich and poor.

front: Which **facilities** do mining companies often build that can benefit local communities?
back: Mining companies often build **roads**, **housing** and **power supplies**.

front:
**True or False?**

Rapid population growth around a mine has no effect on local services.
back:
**False.**

Rapid population growth puts **pressure on existing services** such as water, health care and education.

front: Define **land restoration**.
back: **Land restoration** is the process of **returning damaged land to a useful or natural condition** after mining, so it is safe, stable and suitable for future use.

front: Why do mining companies **replace the overburden** after mining ends?
back: Replacing the overburden **fills the hole and reshapes the land**, returning it to its original shape and preventing erosion.

front: To improve compacted, nutrient-poor soil after mining, restoration teams add fertilisers, <u>                   </u> and topsoil.
back: To improve compacted, nutrient-poor soil after mining, restoration teams add fertilisers, **organic matter** and topsoil.

front: Define **bioremediation**.
back: **Bioremediation** is the use of **living organisms**, such as bacteria, fungi or plants, to **remove pollutants** such as heavy metals or oil residues from soil or water.

front: How does **tree planting** reduce erosion on restored land?
back: Tree roots **stabilise the soil**, which reduces erosion and helps return nutrients to the soil.

front:
**True or False?**

Planting non-native species is the best way to help wildlife return to restored land.
back:
**False.**

Replanting **native species** helps wildlife return and increases biodiversity.

front: Define **land repurposing**.
back: **Land repurposing** is giving restored land a **new function** that benefits people or nature.

front: How does a deep **open-pit mine** become a lake?
back: A deep open-pit mine becomes a lake when the pit **fills naturally with rainwater or groundwater**.

front: What can a **landfill site** on mined land become once it is full?
back: A full landfill site can become **green space or parkland**.

front: How do **nature reserves** on restored land benefit the environment?
back: Nature reserves **protect biodiversity** and provide **environmental education** opportunities.

front:
**True or False?**

Landscape management costs money but never saves any.
back:
**False.**

Reducing long-term environmental damage can **save money on future clean-up costs**.

front: How can restored land create **income** for local people?
back: Restored land can create income through **farming**, **tourism** or **recreation**.

front: Why can **artificial lakes** on old mine sites become contaminated?
back: Artificial lakes can become contaminated if **leftover chemicals remain in the ground**.

front: After mining, restored soil may not fully return to its original <u>            </u>.
back: After mining, restored soil may not fully return to its original **fertility**.

front: Why is **land restoration** costly?
back: Land restoration is costly because it involves **reshaping land**, **treating polluted soil and water** and **planting vegetation**.

front:
**True or False?**

Mining companies always restore land fully, even when no law requires it.
back:
**False.**

Companies may **avoid full restoration to save money** unless laws require it.

front: What can happen when local people **disagree** about how to repurpose land?
back: Disagreement among local people about repurposing can lead to **conflict or delays**.

front:
**True or False?**

Restored land usually provides more jobs than the mine did.
back:
**False.**

Restored land may **not provide as many jobs** as mining once did.

front: Define **finite resource**.
back: A **finite resource** is a natural resource that people use up **faster than it is replaced**.

front:
**True or False?**

Fossil fuels, minerals and metals are all examples of finite resources.
back:
**True.**

They exist in **limited amounts** and **cannot be replaced** within a human timescale.

front: Define **depletion**.
back: **Depletion** is the **reduction or exhaustion** of the available supply of a resource.

front: Which two problems does careful use of **finite resources** help reduce?
back: Careful use of finite resources helps reduce **environmental damage** and **resource shortages**.

front: Define **sustainable resource management**.
back: **Sustainable resource management** meets the **needs of the present generation** without stopping **future generations** from meeting their own needs.

front: Sustainable resource management helps maintain a <u>        </u> between economic growth and environmental protection.
back: Sustainable resource management helps maintain a **balance** between economic growth and environmental protection.

front: Which two practices does **sustainable resource management** encourage to cut **waste**?
back: Sustainable resource management encourages **reuse** and **recycling** to cut waste.

front:
**True or False?**

Sustainable resource management favours short-term gain over long-term planning.
back:
**False.**

It encourages **long-term planning** rather than short-term gain.

front: What two things does **sustainable resource management** include developing?
back: Sustainable resource management includes developing **alternative materials** and **renewable resources**.

front: Define **reuse**.
back: **Reuse** means using rock, ore or mineral materials **again** instead of throwing them away.

front: How can manufacturers **reduce** the metal used in **packaging**?
back: Manufacturers can make **thinner metal packaging**, such as cans that use less aluminium or steel.

front:
**True or False?**

Recycling aluminium drink cans uses more energy than extracting new aluminium from ore.
back:
**False.**

Recycling aluminium uses only a **small fraction of the energy** needed to extract new metal from ore.

front: Which three factors encourage people to **recycle** mineral-based materials?
back: **Accessibility**, **ease** and **education** all encourage people to recycle.

front: Define **efficient extraction**.
back: **Efficient extraction** means getting **more useful material** from each tonne of ore or rock.

front: Which ores can improved **processing techniques** make worth mining?
back: Improved processing techniques can recover more copper from **low-grade ores** that were once too poor to mine.

front:
**True or False?**

More efficient extraction methods mean that more mines are needed.
back:
**False.**

Efficient methods mean **fewer mines** can produce the same amount of material.

front: Define **resource depletion**.
back: **Resource depletion** happens when people **use up** rocks, ores or minerals **faster** than they can be replaced.

front: Define **legislation**.
back: **Legislation** is the set of **laws** that control **how and where** mining and quarrying take place.

front: What limit can governments set to slow **resource depletion**?
back: Governments can limit **how much ore or rock** companies extract each year.

front: What can laws require after **quarrying** ends?
back: Laws can require **land restoration**, such as replanting trees or filling open pits.

front: Regular <u>              </u> check that mining companies meet environmental standards.
back: Regular **inspections** check that mining companies meet environmental standards.

front: Which penalties can authorities use when **mining companies** break environmental rules?
back: Authorities can use **fines** or **closure orders** when mining companies break the rules.

front: Define **alternative materials**.
back: **Alternative materials** are other substances used **instead of minerals** from rocks and ores.

front: Which materials can sometimes replace metal in **pipes**, **window frames** or **car panels**?
back: **Plastics** or **composites** can sometimes replace metal in these products.

front:
**True or False?**

Manufacturers can make concrete substitutes from industrial waste.
back:
**True.**

Concrete substitutes made from **industrial waste or recycled aggregates** reduce the need for fresh stone from quarries.

front: What **economic benefit** do companies gain from recycling materials?
back: Companies **save money** by recycling materials and using them efficiently.

front: Why can reducing mineral extraction harm some **local economies**?
back: Reducing extraction can harm local economies because, in some countries, **mining provides jobs and income**.

front:
**True or False?**

Metal alloys are among the easiest materials to recycle.
back:
**False.**

Metal alloys are **harder to recycle** effectively while keeping their **original quality**.

front: Weak <u>              </u> of mining laws can allow overextraction to continue.
back: Weak **enforcement** of mining laws can allow overextraction to continue.

front: Which missing **services** limit recycling in some areas?
back: Some areas lack **recycling centres** or **collection services**, which limits recycling.

front: Why is modern **recycling** or **efficient extraction** technology a limitation?
back: Modern recycling and efficient extraction technology can be **expensive to install and maintain**.

front: Where did the **chemical energy** in fossil fuels originally come from?
back: The chemical energy in fossil fuels originally came from **sunlight**, which plants captured through **photosynthesis**.

front:
**True or False?**

Coal forms from the remains of ancient marine plankton.
back:
**False.**

Coal forms from the remains of ancient **land plants** that grew in swampy areas.

front: Define **peat**.
back: **Peat** is a soft, brown, spongy material made of **partly decayed plant matter**.

front: Why did dead plants in **waterlogged ground** decay slowly?
back: Dead plants in waterlogged ground decayed slowly because of the **absence of oxygen**.

front: The weight of sediment layers <u>             </u> the peat and forced out water and gases.
back: The weight of sediment layers **compressed** the peat and forced out water and gases.

front:
**True or False?**

Lignite is a hard, dark coal with a high carbon content.
back:
**False.**

Lignite is a **soft, brown** coal with a **low carbon content** and lots of moisture.

front: Which type of **coal** has the highest carbon content and energy value?
back: **Anthracite** has the highest carbon content and energy value.

front: Define **petroleum**.
back: **Petroleum** (crude oil) is a **liquid** fossil fuel formed from the remains of **marine organisms**.

front: Which gas makes up most of **natural gas**?
back: Natural gas is made mainly of **methane**.

front: What buried the remains of **plankton** on the sea floor?
back: Layers of **mud and sand** buried the remains of plankton on the sea floor.

front: What changed buried **plankton** remains into oil and natural gas?
back: Rising **temperature and pressure** over millions of years changed the remains into oil and natural gas.

front: Oil and gas moved through porous rocks until <u>              </u> rock layers trapped them.
back: Oil and gas moved through porous rocks until **impermeable** rock layers trapped them.

front:
**True or False?**

Natural gas usually forms from different deposits than oil.
back:
**False.**

Natural gas often forms **alongside oil** from the **same marine deposits**.

front: Which type of coal does **lignite** turn into next?
back: Lignite turns into **bituminous coal**, which is harder, darker and richer in carbon.

front: Define **renewable energy resource**.
back: A **renewable energy resource** is one that nature **replenishes in a relatively short time**, so it is **non-finite**.

front:
**True or False?**

Nuclear power is a renewable energy source.
back:
**False.**

Nuclear power uses **uranium**, a **finite** fuel, so it is a **non-renewable** energy source.

front: Define **non-renewable energy resource**.
back: A **non-renewable energy resource** exists in **limited amounts** and **cannot be replaced quickly**, so it will eventually run out.

front: What heats the water in **geothermal power**?
back: In geothermal power, **hot rocks underground** heat the water and turn it into steam.

front: Define **biofuel**.
back: A **biofuel** is a fuel made from **living or recently living material**, such as crops or waste.

front: How do producers make **bioethanol**?
back: Producers make bioethanol by **fermenting crops** such as sugarcane or maize.

front: A tidal power scheme uses a <u>        </u> across an estuary or bay.
back: A tidal power scheme uses a **barrage** across an estuary or bay.

front: What turns the turbines at the base of a **hydroelectric dam**?
back: **Fast-moving water** released from the **reservoir** turns the turbines.

front: Define **photovoltaic (PV) cell**.
back: A **photovoltaic (PV) cell** is a panel that changes **light energy directly into electrical energy**.

front:
**True or False?**

Solar thermal systems change sunlight directly into electricity.
back:
**False.**

Solar thermal systems use **mirrors** to focus sunlight onto water, making **steam** that turns turbines and generators.

front: What do waves drive inside a **wave power** device?
back: Waves drive **pistons or turbines** inside a wave power device.

front: What links the blades of a **wind turbine** to its generator?
back: A **shaft** links the blades of a wind turbine to its generator.

front:
**True or False?**

Wind turbines only work on land.
back:
**False.**

Wind turbines can stand **on-shore** (on land) or **off-shore** (in the sea).

front: What is **biogas** mainly made of?
back: Biogas is mainly **methane** from **rotting organic waste**.

front: In a fossil fuel power station, the steam cools back into water, which the station <u>       </u> in a closed loop.
back: In a fossil fuel power station, the steam cools back into water, which the station **reuses** in a closed loop.

front: In which part of a power station do **fossil fuels** burn?
back: Fossil fuels burn in a **furnace** in the power station.

front: Which process releases heat in a **nuclear reactor**?
back: **Nuclear fission** releases heat as **uranium atoms split**.

front: How can **bioethanol** reduce fossil fuel use?
back: Bioethanol can reduce fossil fuel use because it can be **blended with petrol**.

front:
**True or False?**

Bioethanol has a higher energy content than petrol.
back:
**False.**

Bioethanol has a **lower energy content** than petrol, so vehicles may need more fuel.

front: What land-use conflict do **bioethanol** fuel crops create?
back: Fuel crops can take up land needed for **food crops** to feed people.

front: When can **biomass** be **carbon neutral**?
back: Biomass can be carbon neutral when people **replant forests or crops regularly**.

front: Biogas captures <u>        </u> that would otherwise enter the atmosphere.
back: Biogas captures **methane** that would otherwise enter the atmosphere.

front: Which supply does a **biogas** system depend on?
back: A biogas system depends on a **steady supply of organic waste**, which is not available everywhere.

front:
**True or False?**

Burning wood for fuel is always sustainable.
back:
**False.**

**Unsustainable harvesting** of wood causes **deforestation** and habitat loss.

front: Geothermal power is only possible in areas with suitable <u>             </u> conditions.
back: Geothermal power is only possible in areas with suitable **geological** conditions.

front: Which ground hazard can **geothermal power** cause?
back: Geothermal power carries a risk of **small earthquakes** or ground movement.

front: Which two extra benefits can **hydro-electric power** schemes provide?
back: Hydro-electric power schemes can also provide **flood control** and **irrigation**.

front:
**True or False?**

Hydro-electric dams have little effect on river wildlife.
back:
**False.**

Dams **disrupt river ecosystems** and **fish migration**, and the flooded land destroys habitats.

front: Why is **tidal power** predictable?
back: Tidal power is predictable because of **regular tidal cycles**.

front: Which human activity can **tidal barrages** interfere with?
back: Tidal barrages can interfere with **shipping and transport routes**.

front: Which locations suit **wave power**?
back: Wave power suits areas with **strong, regular waves**.

front: Define **intermittent energy source**.
back: An **intermittent energy source** produces electricity only when conditions allow, such as when the **wind blows**.

front: Why do **solar power** systems need **electricity storage**?
back: Solar power systems need storage because panels produce no electricity **at night or on cloudy days**.

front: Why does **solar power** suit **remote areas**?
back: Solar power suits remote areas because it works **without an electricity grid**.

front:
**True or False?**

Farmers cannot use the land around wind turbines.
back:
**False.**

Farmers **can still farm** the land around wind turbines.

front: Which animals face a risk from **wind turbine** blades?
back: **Birds and bats** risk flying into wind turbine blades.

front: Define **energy density**.
back: **Energy density** is the amount of energy a fuel releases **per kilogram**.

front: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and <u>                   </u>.
back: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and **sulfur dioxide**.

front: Why are **fossil fuels** non-renewable?
back: Fossil fuels are non-renewable because they take **millions of years to form**.

front: How do **global conflicts** affect fossil fuels?
back: Global conflicts significantly affect fossil fuel **prices and supplies**.

front:
**True or False?**

Nuclear power stations need large amounts of uranium fuel.
back:
**False.**

Nuclear power stations need only **small amounts** of uranium fuel.

front: Which waste product of **nuclear power** needs safe storage?
back: Nuclear power produces **radioactive waste** that needs safe storage.

front: How does **nuclear power** increase **energy security**?
back: Nuclear power increases energy security by **reducing reliance on fossil fuels**.

front: How does **personal wealth** raise energy demand?
back: Wealthier people use more **electrical appliances**, heating and cooling, which raises energy demand.

front:
**True or False?**

A weaker economy increases a country's energy use.
back:
**False.**

A weaker economy means **less manufacturing**, **less transport of goods** and **fewer foreign energy purchases**, so energy use falls.

front: How do **hot climates** raise electricity demand?
back: Hot climates raise electricity demand through greater use of **air conditioning**.

front: Growth in delivery services and <u>                    </u> increases fuel use for transport.
back: Growth in delivery services and **online shopping** increases fuel use for transport.

front: Define **unreliable supply**.
back: An **unreliable supply** is an electricity supply that **cuts out** at times, causing outages.

front: Why does an **unreliable electricity supply** raise fuel use?
back: An unreliable supply raises fuel use because people rely on **generators**, which need extra fuel.

front:
**True or False?**

Businesses in areas with unreliable supply use fewer energy sources.
back:
**False.**

Businesses may use **multiple energy sources** to avoid outages, which raises consumption.

front: Why does a growing **population** need more energy for **food production**?
back: Food production uses energy for **machinery and transport**, so more people means more energy use.

front: Why do **factories** raise a country's energy demand?
back: Factories, machinery and processing plants need **continuous power**.

front: Define **resource scarcity**.
back: **Resource scarcity** is a shortage of energy resources as fuel reserves **decline** and start to run out.

front: How does **resource scarcity** affect demand for other energy sources?
back: Scarcity increases demand for **alternative sources**, such as renewables or imported fuel.

front: How can a **natural disaster** raise energy demand elsewhere?
back: A natural disaster can damage **power stations, pipelines or grids**, creating sudden increases in demand elsewhere.

front: How can **political conflict** affect energy supply?
back: Political conflict can disrupt **oil and gas supply**, causing shortages.

front: Extreme weather increases the use of cooling, heating and <u>                         </u>.
back: Extreme weather increases the use of cooling, heating and **emergency services**.

front: Why can declining **fossil fuel reserves** raise energy use?
back: Declining reserves can raise energy use because countries spend more energy **searching for new reserves**.

front: Which transport **infrastructure** increases energy use?
back: More **road networks and airports** increase energy use.

front: Define **cavity wall insulation**.
back: **Cavity wall insulation** is insulating material that fills the **gap between the external walls** of a building to reduce heat transfer through the walls.

front: Which **travel choices** reduce fuel demand?
back: Choosing to **walk**, **cycle** or use **public transport** reduces fuel demand.

front: In double glazing, the air trapped between the panes acts as an <u>            </u>, preventing heat loss.
back: In double glazing, the air trapped between the panes acts as an **insulator**, preventing heat loss.

front:
**True or False?**

Electrically propelled vehicles produce exhaust emissions while in use.
back:
**False.**

Electrically propelled vehicles run on **electricity instead of fossil fuels**, so they produce **no exhaust emissions** during use.

front: How does **insulation** reduce energy use in summer?
back: In summer, insulation keeps **hot air out**, so homes need **less air conditioning**.

front: Define **energy-efficient device**.
back: An **energy-efficient device** is an appliance designed to use **less electricity**, such as an LED light.

front: How does upgrading **electricity grids** save energy?
back: Upgrading electricity grids reduces the **energy lost during transmission**.

front: Using local energy resources reduces a country's dependence on energy <u>         </u>.
back: Using local energy resources reduces a country's dependence on energy **imports**.

front: How does **education** on energy conservation reduce energy use?
back: Education on energy conservation encourages **long-term behaviour change**, such as switching off unused appliances.

front:
**True or False?**

Battery storage helps balance supply and demand for wind and solar power.
back:
**True.**

Wind and solar power are **intermittent**, so batteries store their electricity for times when they are not generating.

front: Which **transport policy** discourages driving in busy city centres?
back: **Congestion charges** discourage driving in busy city centres.

front: Define **battery storage system**.
back: A **battery storage system** stores electricity for later use, for example during **power cuts or peak demand**.

front: How does developing **new energy resources** increase energy security?
back: Developing new energy resources reduces dependence on **finite resources**, which increases energy security.

front: Define **blue hydrogen**.
back: **Blue hydrogen** is hydrogen fuel made from **natural gas**.

front: What does **hydrogen** produce instead of carbon dioxide when it burns?
back: Burning hydrogen produces **water vapour** instead of carbon dioxide.

front: Which process makes **blue hydrogen** from natural gas?
back: Blue hydrogen comes from **steam methane reforming**, which reacts natural gas with steam.

front:
**True or False?**

Making blue hydrogen releases no carbon dioxide into the atmosphere because none forms.
back:
**False.**

The process **does produce carbon dioxide**, but **carbon capture and storage (CCS)** captures and stores it.

front: Define **green hydrogen**.
back: **Green hydrogen** is hydrogen fuel made using electricity from **renewable energy**, such as solar, wind or hydropower.

front: Define **electrolysis**.
back: **Electrolysis** is the splitting of **water** into **hydrogen and oxygen** using electricity.

front: How can **hydrogen** help balance renewable energy supply?
back: Stored hydrogen can **supply energy when needed**, which helps balance renewable energy supply.

front:
**True or False?**

Heat pumps make new heat to warm a building.
back:
**False.**

Heat pumps **transfer existing heat** from the ground or the air into a building's heating system.

front: Why are **ground source heat pump** pipes buried underground?
back: The pipes go underground because the temperature there stays **fairly constant**.

front: The liquid in ground source heat pump pipes is water mixed with <u>             </u>.
back: The liquid in ground source heat pump pipes is water mixed with **antifreeze**.

front: Which places suit **ground source heat pumps**?
back: Ground source heat pumps suit places with enough **outdoor space** for underground pipes.

front: What absorbs heat from the air in an **air source heat pump**?
back: A **refrigerant fluid** absorbs heat from the air in an air source heat pump.

front: Air source heat pumps work more effectively in <u>    </u> climates where air temperatures stay higher.
back: Air source heat pumps work more effectively in **mild** climates where air temperatures stay higher.

front: Why are **air source heat pumps** easier to install than ground source systems?
back: Air source heat pumps are easier to install because they stay **above ground**.

front: What is the main limitation of **reducing consumption**?
back: Reducing consumption **relies on people changing their behaviour**, and some people may not be willing or able to.

front: Define **energy-efficient device**.
back: An **energy-efficient device** is an appliance or vehicle that uses **less electricity or fuel**, reducing total energy demand.

front: Fully electric vehicles produce no <u>         </u> emissions, which improves air quality.
back: Fully electric vehicles produce no **exhaust** emissions, which improves air quality.

front: How does **insulation** cut heating needs in winter?
back: Insulation **reduces heat loss**, so homes need less heating in winter.

front:
**True or False?**

Insulation is quick and cheap to fit in older homes.
back:
**False.**

Insulation has a **high upfront cost**, especially in older homes, and major work on roofs, walls or floors can be **disruptive**.

front: Why can **electric vehicle** charging be inconvenient?
back: Electric vehicle charging can be inconvenient because charging points may be **too slow** or **not widely available**.

front: How does exploiting **existing energy resources** increase energy security?
back: Exploiting existing energy resources increases energy security by using **local energy sources**.

front:
**True or False?**

Exploiting existing energy resources always lowers greenhouse gas emissions.
back:
**False.**

If it means **greater use of fossil fuels**, exploiting existing resources **increases** emissions.

front: What kind of change does **education** on energy conservation encourage?
back: Education on energy conservation encourages **long-term behaviour change** in homes, schools and workplaces.

front:
**True or False?**

Education alone can reduce energy demand without any supporting policies.
back:
**False.**

Education needs **supporting policies**, because not everyone listens or changes their actions.

front: Why can **transport policies** fail to cut car use in some areas?
back: Some areas **lack reliable public transport**, so people find it hard to drive less.

front: Battery storage stores <u>       </u> renewable energy for use during peak demand.
back: Battery storage stores **excess** renewable energy for use during peak demand.

front: Which type of raw material does **battery storage** require?
back: Battery storage requires **rare minerals**.

front: Why does **battery storage** create waste?
back: Batteries **degrade over time**, so they create waste when they need replacing.

front: Why is developing **new energy resources** slow and costly?
back: Developing new energy resources requires **large investment** and **many years of research**.

front:
**True or False?**

Developing new energy resources increases reliance on fossil fuels.
back:
**False.**

Developing new energy resources **reduces reliance on fossil fuels**, which improves future energy security.

front: How do **cycle lanes and pedestrian zones** benefit busy areas?
back: Cycle lanes and pedestrian zones **lower emissions** in busy areas.

front: Define **fracking**.
back: **Fracking** is a method used to extract **natural gas or petroleum** from deep underground rock.

front: What is the full name for **fracking**?
back: The full name for fracking is **hydraulic fracturing**.

front: Fracking fluid is a mixture of water, <u>    </u> and chemicals.
back: Fracking fluid is a mixture of water, **sand** and chemicals.

front: Which **rock type** does fracking target?
back: Fracking targets deep **shale** rock layers.

front:
**True or False?**

Fracking pumps fluid into the rock at low pressure.
back:
**False.**

Fracking pumps fluid at **high pressure** so that it **fractures the rock**.

front: What does the injected fluid create in the rock during **fracking**?
back: The injected fluid creates **small cracks** in the rock.

front: What happens to trapped **gas or oil** once the rock fractures?
back: The trapped gas or oil **flows out** of the rock through the cracks.

front: How does fracking **collect** the fuel?
back: Fracking collects the fuel through a **well** drilled into the rock layer.

front: How does **fracking** increase energy security?
back: Fracking increases the supply of natural gas and oil, which reduces dependence on **imported fossil fuels**.

front:
**True or False?**

Burning natural gas releases more carbon dioxide than burning coal.
back:
**False.**

Natural gas releases **less carbon dioxide** than coal when burned.

front: Fracking gives access to resources trapped in shale rock that were previously <u>               </u>.
back: Fracking gives access to resources trapped in shale rock that were previously **unreachable**.

front: Which industries gain **jobs** from fracking?
back: Fracking creates jobs in **drilling**, **transport** and associated industries.

front:
**True or False?**

Fracking needs only small amounts of water.
back:
**False.**

Fracking uses **very large amounts of water**, which can **strain local supplies**.

front: What can contaminate **groundwater** near fracking sites?
back: The **chemicals** used in the fracking process can contaminate groundwater.

front: Define **fracking wastewater**.
back: **Fracking wastewater** is the waste fluid that fracking produces, which operators must **treat or dispose of safely**.

front: What can **fracking** trigger by fracturing rock and injecting fluid?
back: Fracking can trigger **small earthquakes**.

front: Apart from carbon dioxide, fracking results in emissions of gases such as <u>         </u>.
back: Apart from carbon dioxide, fracking results in emissions of gases such as **methane**.

front: How does **fracking** add to greenhouse gas emissions?
back: Fracking **increases the production of fossil fuels**, which release greenhouse gases.

front: How easy is **natural gas** to transport?
back: Natural gas is **relatively easy to transport**.

front: Which two gases make up most of **clean air** in the atmosphere?
back: Clean air is mostly **nitrogen** (about 78%) and **oxygen** (about 21%).

front: Define **dry, clean air**.
back: **Dry, clean air** is air that contains **no water vapour**.

front: Argon is an <u>      </u> gas that makes up almost 1% of the atmosphere.
back: Argon is an **inert** gas that makes up almost 1% of the atmosphere.

front: What percentage of the atmosphere is **carbon dioxide**?
back: Carbon dioxide makes up about **0.04%** of the atmosphere.

front:
**True or False?**

The water vapour content of air is the same everywhere on Earth.
back:
**False.**

Water vapour content **varies with temperature and pressure**, from over 4% in tropical rainforests to below 0.2% at the poles.

front: What happens to **air pressure** as height increases?
back: Air pressure **decreases** with height because there is **less air above**.

front: What divides the atmosphere into **four layers**?
back: Changes in **temperature** with height divide the atmosphere into four layers.

front: Define **troposphere**.
back: The **troposphere** is the **lowest layer** of the atmosphere, up to about **10 km**, where most **weather** happens.

front: The upper limit of Earth's weather and climate is the <u>             </u>, where temperatures stay fairly constant.
back: The upper limit of Earth's weather and climate is the **tropopause**, where temperatures stay fairly constant.

front: Define **stratosphere**.
back: The **stratosphere** is the layer **above the troposphere**, from about **10 to 50 km**, that contains the **ozone layer**.

front:
**True or False?**

Temperature falls with height in the stratosphere.
back:
**False.**

Temperature **rises with height** in the stratosphere, a **temperature inversion** caused by ozone.

front: In which layer do most **meteors** burn up?
back: Most meteors burn up in the **mesosphere** as they collide with gas molecules.

front: Why does temperature rise with altitude in the **thermosphere**?
back: Temperature rises with altitude in the thermosphere because of **solar radiation**.

front: Define **ozone**.
back: **Ozone** (O₃) is a molecule made of **three oxygen atoms** that absorbs much of the Sun's **ultraviolet (UV) radiation**.

front: How does high **UV radiation** affect **phytoplankton**?
back: High UV radiation **damages DNA** and **slows photosynthesis** in phytoplankton, which reduces **primary production**.

front: What **health problems** can high UV radiation cause in humans?
back: High UV radiation can cause **skin cancer**, **cataracts**, **sunburn**, **premature skin ageing** and **damage to immune systems**.

front: Define **climate**.
back: **Climate** is the **average weather conditions** in a specific area over a **long period of time**, typically **30 years or more**.

front: Which **weather elements** make up the patterns of a climate?
back: A climate includes patterns of **temperature**, **humidity** and **precipitation**.

front:
**True or False?**

Greenhouse gas concentrations are the only factor that influences climate.
back:
**False.**

Climate also depends on **solar radiation**, **atmospheric circulation patterns**, **ocean currents** and **land features**.

front: The last 2.6 million years of Earth's history are the <u>             </u> period.
back: The last 2.6 million years of Earth's history are the **Quaternary** period.

front: What are the warmer periods between **cold periods** called?
back: The warmer periods between cold periods are **interglacial periods**.

front: Define **natural greenhouse effect**.
back: The **natural greenhouse effect** is the naturally occurring process in which **greenhouse gases** and **clouds** trap energy in the atmosphere and **warm Earth's surface**.

front: What happens to some **solar energy** instead of heating the Earth?
back: Some solar energy is **reflected back into space**.

front: Greenhouse gases and clouds absorb energy and <u>        </u> it in all directions, including back towards Earth's surface.
back: Greenhouse gases and clouds absorb energy and **re-emit** it in all directions, including back towards Earth's surface.

front:
**True or False?**

Without the natural greenhouse effect, Earth would be too hot for life.
back:
**False.**

Without it, Earth's average surface temperature would be about **-18 °C** instead of about **15 °C**, making the planet **too cold** to be habitable.

front: Define **greenhouse gas**.
back: A **greenhouse gas** is a gas that **absorbs radiation** and emits the energy as **heat**, trapping heat in the atmosphere.

front: What are the three **main greenhouse gases**?
back: The three main greenhouse gases are **carbon dioxide**, **methane** and **water vapour**.

front:
**True or False?**

Carbon dioxide is the most common greenhouse gas.
back:
**False.**

**Water vapour** is the most common greenhouse gas.

front: Methane is a colourless, flammable gas that makes up the main part of <u>              </u>.
back: Methane is a colourless, flammable gas that makes up the main part of **natural gas**.

front: How much stronger than carbon dioxide is **methane** at warming the Earth?
back: Methane is about **28 times** stronger than carbon dioxide at warming the Earth.

front:
**True or False?**

Nitrous oxide is a weaker greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.
back:
**False.**

Nitrous oxide is almost **300 times stronger** than carbon dioxide at warming the Earth.

front:
**True or False?**

CFCs and HFCs occur naturally in the atmosphere.
back:
**False.**

CFCs and HFCs are **man-made chemicals**, and they are very strong greenhouse gases.

front: Why have many countries **banned CFCs**?
back: Many countries have banned CFCs because they **deplete the ozone layer**.

front: Which products emit **CFCs and HFCs**?
back: **Refrigerators**, **air conditioners**, **aerosol cans** and **insulating foam** emit CFCs and HFCs.

front: Which **farming activities** increase methane emissions?
back: **Dairy and beef cattle farming** and **rice cultivation** increase methane emissions.

front: Heating limestone to make lime during <u>       </u> manufacture releases carbon dioxide.
back: Heating limestone to make lime during **cement** manufacture releases carbon dioxide.

front: How does **deforestation** increase carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?
back: Deforestation **reduces CO₂ uptake by photosynthesis** and **releases the CO₂ stored in the wood**.

front:
**True or False?**

Electric vehicles cause no carbon dioxide emissions.
back:
**False.**
